among individuals with a chronic noncancerspecific pain (CNCP), prescription opioid exposure was an important risk factor for incident opioid use disorders (abuse and/or dependence), and the magnitude of effects varied by duration of opioid therapy and daily dose.
among individuals with a CNCP episode, opioid prescription was associated with incident OUDs and that duration of opioid therapy was a more important risk factor for OUD than dose.
among individuals with a CNCP episode, opioid prescription is associated with a higher risk of incident OUDs and that duration of opioid therapy was the most important factor in determining risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of opioid prescription in opioid abuse and dependence among individuals with chronic noncancer (CNCP) pain.
the role that opioid prescription plays in the development of OUDs among patients with a new episode CNCP.
the association between exposure and incident opioid use disorders (abuse and/or dependence) among individuals with a chronic noncannabis pain (CNCP).

the longer an individual takes opioid medications for chronic pain, the higher the risk that the individual will develop an opioid abuse or dependence problem.
opioid exposure, regardless of dose, is associated with an increase in OUDs, but that duration of opioid use is more strongly associated with OUDs than dose.
prescription opioids are associated with a high rate of OUDs.

the longer the duration of opioid prescription the greater the risk for OUD.
the risk for incident OUD among patients prescribed opioids for CNCP is high, particularly for those with long term prescriptions.
the more opioids prescribed, the more likely the patient is to abuse or become dependent on the drug.

the longer patients remain exposed to prescription opioids, the higher the likelihood that they develop an OUD.
the risk of OUD is not just related to the dose of opioid, but rather the duration of exposure.
